title: Before Udaypur: Prehistory, Early Vidisha and the Historical Landscape of Central India

sections.title: Old ground, older names
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows the limits of the oldest evidence and what the country was called before Udaypur existed: - stone tools from the valleys of the Betwa and its tributaries; - a chalcolithic mound somewhere in the district, and a sequence around Vidisha running from the Chalcolithic to the early medieval; - nothing prehistoric recorded on Udaypur's own hill; - the country's names: Daśārṇa in literary tradition and Ākara in inscriptions. Vidisha was its capital, so the hill stood in a named country whose centre was elsewhere.
sections.transition: That centre was a city in the fork of the rivers downstream.

paras.first: The oldest human traces in the country around Udaypur lie in its river valleys.
paras.last: The caves on Shiva Pindi are recorded, some natural and some made by people, but nothing in that record speaks of their use in those ages.
paras.plan_title: Tools in the valleys, nothing on the hill
paras.plan_point: - The oldest human traces in this country are district finds: palaeolithic choppers, handaxes and cleavers from the valleys of the Betwa, Bina, Dhasan and Keothan. - A chalcolithic mound in the district, its wares dated 1000–700 BC, also yielded microliths. - Explorations around Vidisha in 1963–65 found cultures from the Chalcolithic to the early medieval. Nothing prehistoric is recorded on Udaypur's hill. Its caves, already familiar from the hill's geology, have no recorded early use. Say this once, as a limit of the evidence and not as a mystery. Do not locate the mound, and do not equate the Keothan with any stream near Udaypur.

paras.first: The country’s literary name was Daśārṇa, current from the days of the Buddha to those of Kālidāsa in about the fifth century CE, and the name still lives in the Dhasan, which rises in the Bhopal country, runs through Bundelkhand and empties into the Betwa.
paras.last: Kauṭilya, minister of Chandragupta Maurya, used the same name; the country reached across eastern Malwa onto the Sagar plateau, cut by the deep valleys of the Dhasan and its headwaters, and its capital was Vidisha, or Besnagar.
paras.plan_point: - The country had names long before the town. In literary geography it was Daśārṇa, from the Buddha's day to Kālidāsa's, with Vidisha as its capital; the name survives in the Dhasan, which joins the Betwa. - Inscriptions call eastern Malwa Ākara, distinct from Avanti in the west. The Nasik praśasti lists both among the lands a Sātavāhana king claimed from Nahapāna: a claim of conquest, told as such. Vidisha was the capital of the Ākara-janapada. - Purāṇic tradition gives the region's first rulers, a Haihaya branch and then the Pradyotas: one sentence, as tradition. For Udaypur, this places the hill in a country that was named, ruled and remembered from a centre some way off.

paras.first: Inscriptions used another name.
paras.last: Before the inscriptions, a branch of the Haihayas is said to have ruled at Vidisha, a city counted in Central India next only to Mahishmati for its antiquity, and by about the sixth century BCE the Pradyotas held a territory commonly called Avanti, though parts of it went by the names Ākara and Daśārṇa; under Caṇḍa Pradyota Ujjayinī in the west first rose to prominence.

sections.title: The old centre and its roads
sections.plan_title: The old centre and its roads
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows Vidisha as the country's centre for more than a thousand years: - a walled city lived in from before Northern Black Polished ware to post-Gupta times; - the Śuṅga capital of Ākara; - rich from the roads that crossed there. The roads it stood on still ran in the eleventh century. The city is the measure of what Udaypur was not: the region's old centre, in which the hill had no recorded part.
sections.transition: The city's shrines began a tradition of worship in stone that later reached the hills around Udaypur.

paras.first: Besnagar, the ancient city in the fork of the rivers, was old long before any king put his name to Udaypur.
paras.last: By the Buddha’s day Vidisha already joined the towns of the Gangetic plains to the western coast and the Deccan, and it grew in standing under Ashoka.
paras.plan_point: - Besnagar (Vessanagar in the Pali books, Vidisha in Sanskrit) was lived in across six periods, from before Northern Black Polished ware to post-Gupta times. - It was walled, probably from the second century BC. - Under the Śuṅgas it was the capital of Ākara. In Kālidāsa's play the crown prince Agnimitra governs there: literary memory, told as such. - By the Gupta age it was still a prosperous town, and its monuments make the district the richest in antiquities in Madhya Bharat. Chapter 2 already set the city in the fork of the rivers: refer to it as "the city in the fork" and do not explain the fork again. Give no distance from Udaypur (Chapter 1 gives the settled range).

paras.first: Kālidāsa’s literary romance *Mālavikāgnimitra* remembers the crown prince Agnimitra serving as viceroy at Vidisha in the reign of his father Puṣyamitra.
paras.last: Until the age of the Guptas, in the fifth century CE, Vidisha remained a flourishing town, and its monuments are centred on the old site and on Udayagiri to the west.

paras.first: The city’s wealth came from where it stood, at the crossing of two important trade routes.
paras.last: None of these accounts mentions Udaypur’s hill.
paras.plan_point: - The city's wealth came from where it stood, at the crossing of two trade routes: one from Pratiṣṭhāna through Ujjayinī and Vidisha to Kauśāmbī, and a branch down the Betwa valley. - It was a town of merchants on the caravan road from Śrāvastī through Kauśāmbī towards Avanti. - The great stūpa at Sanchi was raised largely from the donations of Vidisha's merchants, though general belief credits Ashoka. Frame that disagreement around the monument, in a clause. - The roads outlived the city: Nemawar lay on the route from the north to the Deccan in the early eleventh century. Do not say or imply that Udaypur lay on these routes. No item says so.

paras.first: That wealth went into monuments.
paras.last: Under the Śuṅgas the city was also a great religious centre for Hindus and Buddhists alike, as the ruins at Sanchi and the many Hindu antiquities from its old site show.

sections.title: Carved rock and early shrines
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows the country around Udaypur as one of the oldest landscapes of worship in stone: - Besnagar's early Vaiṣṇava shrine, its lime mortar and the Garuḍa pillar a Greek king's envoy set up before it; - early Śaiva images; - the Gupta rock-cut shrines at Udayagiri; - small Gupta-form shrines at Badoh and Ramgarh; - a fifth-century panel of the Seven Mothers, with a contemporary inscription, cut into the hill between Badoh and Pathari, on the far slope of Udaypur's own range. On Udaypur's hill the survey dates a cave, with unfinished figures believed to be Jain Tīrthaṅkaras, to the sixth century. Tiwari reads Viṣṇu images found between Muradpur and Sonari as Gupta. These are a proposal and a reading. They place the hill inside that landscape without showing that anyone settled there.
sections.transition: Meanwhile the old city itself was emptying.

paras.first: At Vidisha, on the site of a later Bhāgavata temple, an elliptical temple of Viṣṇu has come to light, early archaeological evidence of Vaiṣṇava worship, believed to have stood at least by the third century BCE.
paras.last: Another early Brāhmī inscription, of the twelfth year of a king Bhāgavata, records a flagstaff set up to Viṣṇu in the temple at Vidisha by one Gautamīputra.
paras.plan_point: - Besnagar has the earliest archaeological evidence of a Vaiṣṇava temple: an elliptical shrine, possibly of timber, with a stone fence and a brick foundation containing the earliest historical lime mortar. - Before it, Heliodorus, envoy of the Greek king Antialcidas, set up a Garuḍa-dhvaja to Vāsudeva and declared himself a Bhāgavata. Its date is a range: first or second century BC, with 140 BC from the Greek king's chronology; the readings go in one note. The pillar is of the region's Vindhyan sandstone, the stone Chapter 2 traced to Udaypur's hill: refer back by content. - Its colossal free-standing statues are dated anywhere from pre-Mauryan to Śuṅga times; give that as a range. - Its images of Durgā, the Seven Mothers and one-faced liṅgas are the earliest Śaiva images in the region. They date to the fourth century AD, or perhaps a century earlier. Śaiva worship in stone in this country is centuries older than the Paramāras. State it as a fact of dates, not as a cause of anything at Udaypur. Not a catalogue of antiquities: three things (the shrine, the pillar, the Śaiva images), each in a sentence or two. (Plan note, run 2.)

paras.first: Besnagar’s colossal statues, three identical *yakṣiṇī*s and a Kubera recovered from the Betwa among them, have been assigned to any age from the pre-Mauryan to the Śuṅga.
paras.last: Stone images of Śiva’s cult were thus standing in this country many centuries before the Paramāras.

paras.first: Gupta kings made their power felt around Vidisha and cut their worship into its hills.
paras.last: More than a dozen flat-roofed shrines, each a sanctum with a two-pillared portico and a monolithic slab roof, have been found at Ramgarh, Chhapara and Badoh in this district.
paras.plan_title: Gupta kings cut into the hills
paras.plan_point: - The Allahabad inscription claims Samudragupta's victory over the Nāga rulers: a royal claim. - Two inscriptions at Udayagiri attest Chandragupta II's sovereignty, one dated Gupta year 82 (AD 401). Its caves include the earliest Brahmanical rock-cut temple and the Varāha panel. - Small flat-roofed shrines continuing the early Gupta form have been found at Ramgarh, Chhapara and Badoh in this district. Never connect Udayagiri with Udaypur by name.

paras.first: Badoh brings the carved landscape onto Udaypur’s own range.
paras.last: In the south face of the hill between Badoh and Pathari, a panel of the Seven Mothers was sculptured in the fifth century, and a contemporary Sanskrit inscription is engraved on a rock-cut tablet beneath it.
paras.plan_point: - **The nearest dated work:** a fifth-century panel of the Seven Mothers, with a contemporary Sanskrit inscription, cut into the south face of the hill between Badoh and Pathari. Pathari stands near the eastern slopes of the range in whose western foothills Udaypur lies. - **Udaypur's own hill:** the survey dates a cave to the sixth century. Its unfinished figures are "believed" to be Jain Tīrthaṅkaras, and its two lines of inscription remain undeciphered. The caves are already known to the reader; this is the one the survey dates. - **Tiwari's surmise:** from Viṣṇu images found between Muradpur and Sonari, Tiwari infers that building went on here five centuries before Udayāditya. Attribute it as Tiwari's reading, a matter of memory and interpretation. These are a proposal and a reading. They place the hill inside the region's carved landscape. Whether anyone lived on it before the Paramāras is the question Chapter 1 leaves open; refer to it in a clause and do not re-argue it.

paras.first: On Udaypur’s hill itself the record is a proposal.
paras.last: A proposed date and a modern surmise set the hill inside the carved country around it, without showing that anyone lived on it before the Paramāras.

sections.title: From Vidisha to Bhilsa
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows four things about the change from Vidisha to Bhilsa: - the old capital was still a royal seat in 608; - it was deserted at some point between the seventh and tenth centuries, and Bhilsa rose on the east bank, its walls said to be built from the old city's stone; - Bhilsa was named for a Sun image, Bhāillasvāmin, whose name is recorded from 878; - in the twelfth century the province around Udaypur carried that name.
sections.transition: By then the powers that mattered on Udaypur's range were nearer than Vidisha had ever been.

paras.first: In 608 the old city was still a seat of royal business.
paras.last: By the tenth century a new town, Bhilsa, stood on the other side of the river, and the old one was almost wholly deserted.
paras.plan_title: The last of the old city
paras.plan_point: - The Kalachuri king Buddharāja issued his grant of 608 from Vaidiśa: the old city was still a seat of royal business. - It was then deserted, and Bhilsa rose across the river. The dating runs from after the seventh century (with a deluge or a political catastrophe proposed) through the eighth or ninth, to "by the tenth". One account has Bhilsa as a branch-town from the ninth. - Bhilsa's outer walls are said to have been built from the old city's square stones: reported, not established. Give the change as a range around the event. The readings go in one note.

paras.first: Between those two points, readings of the old city’s end differ.
paras.last: Whatever the date, the new town is said to have flourished at the old city’s cost, and stones from Besnagar are said to have gone into its outer walls of square stone.

paras.first: The new town did not take the old city’s name.
paras.last: Bhoja’s *Śṛṅgāramañjarīkathā* is said to treat Bhailasvamipur as one part of Vidisha, and the corrupted form of that name later became a synonym for the city as a whole.
paras.plan_title: A town named for the Sun
paras.plan_point: - Bhilsa took its name from Bhāillasvāmin, an image of the Sun worshipped in a temple there. In the CII editor's reading, the name means "the store-house of lustre". - The name is first recorded in 878. - The Sun temple was standing in the tenth century: an inscription of the reign of a king Krishna, probably the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Krishna III (939–68), refers to it. The identification is the Gazetteer's "probably"; keep it. - About 1030 Al-Bīrūnī noted that the town bore the name of its idol. Use him here only for the name; Bhilsa's political place is Chapter 2's and Chapter 1's. - The 1172 record places Udayapur in the province called the Bhāillasvāmi-mahādvādaśaka. Recall it in one clause, without explaining the province again. For Udaypur this matters: the name of its later province was a Sun temple's at Bhilsa.

paras.first: The name travelled further than the temple.
paras.last: Udaypur’s later province thus carried the name of a Sun image worshipped at Bhilsa.

sections.title: A frontier on Udaypur’s range
sections.statement: By the end, the reader sees Udaypur's own range as a frontier crowded with temples in the two centuries before the Paramāra foundation: - Malwa passed from the Pratihāras to a Rāṣṭrakūṭa vassal in 808–812, in Ganguly's reading; - a Rāṣṭrakūṭa minister set up a Garuḍa pillar at Pathari in 861; - Gyaraspur, in the same foothills as Udaypur and on the old road to Sagar, had temples of the eighth to tenth centuries; - Badoh–Pathari was a temple town round its tanks, its rulers unknown; - on Udaypur's hill, a two-line inscription is assigned to the eighth century and tentatively read; - the Chandellas claimed Bhilsa by 954, and three dynasties competed for the region. Who held the hill before the Paramāras is not known.
sections.transition: Chapter 4 turns to the Paramāras' arrival in this frontier and the foundation of Udaypur.

paras.first: By the ninth century the powers with a stake in Udaypur’s range were near neighbours.
paras.last: The Pratihāras, who reigned over Malwa for a long time, may have had some sway over this district too, but how far their hold reached here is not known.
paras.plan_point: - Between 808 and 812, Malwa passed from the Gurjara-Pratihāras to a vassal of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas. This is Ganguly's inference, attributed in the note. - The Rāṣṭrakūṭas shared out their conquests north of the Narmada among members of their family, and the plateau near Bhilsa was for a time under their rule. - In 861 the chief minister of a Rāṣṭrakūṭa king, Parabala, set up a Garuḍa-dhvaja at Pathari, on the far slope of Udaypur's range. - How far the Pratihāras held this district is not known.

paras.first: Gyaraspur, Udaypur’s neighbour in the western foothills, lies in a gorge of low steep hills on the old high road to Sagar.
paras.last: The style takes its name from the Gurjara-Pratihāras, under whose sway these regions largely lay in the eighth and ninth centuries.
paras.plan_point: - **Gyaraspur:** in the same western foothills as Udaypur, on the old high road to Sagar, it has monuments of the eighth to tenth centuries. Its Maladevi, partly rock-cut, is a mature temple in the Pratihāra style. - **Badoh:** now a petty village, it was a prosperous medieval town of temples round a large tank, its ruins shared with Pathari. Its Gadarmal keeps a ninth-century basement and porch; a shepherd legend explains the name, as legend. Its Daśāvatāra group runs from the eighth to the tenth century. - **Pathari:** its Varāha and Śiva temple run from the ninth to the eleventh. - Little is known of who ruled Badoh or who built its monuments. Never merge Gyaraspur, Badoh, Pathari and Udaypur into one place, or their dates into one. Not a temple-by-temple inventory: the point is a range crowded with temple towns whose rulers are unknown. (Plan note, run 2.)

paras.first: Badoh is now a petty village, but in the medieval period it was a prosperous town, its temples set mostly round a large tank to the south; a second fine tank and the monuments now counted to neighbouring Pathari belonged to the same old town.
paras.last: Of the rulers of this locality in the medieval period, or of the builders of its monuments, very little is known.

paras.first: On Udaypur’s own hill, a two-line inscription is assigned by the survey to the eighth century CE.
paras.last: It opens with the *siddham* sign, and in a tentative interpretation it mentions a *sūtradhāra* and the names Shurapa and Ghutaddha.
paras.plan_point: The survey assigns a two-line inscription on Udaypur's hill to the eighth century. It opens with the *siddham*, and in the survey's tentative reading it names a *sūtradhāra*. This is a proposal, stated as one; Chapter 1 weighs what it can bear, so do not re-argue it here. It is a different inscription from the cave's undeciphered lines in 3.3: never connect the two. A short paragraph.

paras.first: A Khajuraho inscription of 954 claims that the Candella kingdom of Jejākabhukti then reached as far as Bhāsvat, which is Bhilsa, on the south-western edge of Candella territory.
paras.last: Who held the hill itself in those years is not known.
paras.plan_point: - The Khajuraho inscription of 954 claims that the Chandella kingdom reached Bhilsa, under Dhaṅga (954–1002): a royal claim. - As Pratihāra power faded, the Chandellas, the Kalachuris of Dāhala and the Paramāras of Malwa administered parts of this region at the same time, competing in war and in building temples. Central India was "thickly studded" with temples, of which a small fraction survives. End on the contested frontier around Udaypur's hill by the late tenth century. Hand on by content. Do not re-introduce the Paramāras as a polity, Dhārā, or Bhilsa as the kingdom's eastern limit.

opening: The oldest human traces in the country around Udaypur lie in its river valleys.
closing: Who held the hill itself in those years is not known.
opening_para: The oldest human traces in the country around Udaypur lie in its river valleys.
